summary: Creates a number of OSPF registries and gives IANA guidance for assigning code points in them. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Many OSPF messages use numbered codes. This note says who keeps the lists of numbers and how new ones are added.

questions: how are ospf code points assigned
subtitle: IANA guidance for assigning code points in OSPF protocols.

tldr.problem: OSPF uses many code points for options, message types, and fields. Without centralized registries, vendors could use the same numbers for different things, breaking interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4940 defines registries for OSPF code points and establishes assignment policies: Standards Action (published RFCs), Experimentation (vendor testing), Vendor Private Use (vendor extensions), and Reserved (future definition).
tldr.outcome: Clear, centralized administration of OSPF code point assignments ensures vendors extend OSPF consistently.

today: RFC 4940 is a Best Current Practice and remains in effect. It provides the framework for OSPF code point assignments at IANA.

sections.title: Why Registries Matter for OSPF
sections.content:
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a routing protocol where routers communicate their view of the network. OSPF messages contain code points, numerical fields indicating message type, options, or properties.

Without centralized management, vendors extending OSPF might assign the same code point to different features, breaking compatibility. RFC 4940 creates IANA registries that maintain code point assignments and policies. This ensures OSPF extensions coexist safely and the protocol can evolve without chaos.
sections.eli5: OSPF is how routers tell each other about the network. An IANA registry keeps code numbers organized so no two people use the same number for different things.

sections.title: Assignment Policies
sections.content:
The RFC uses standard terminology for assignment policies. Standards Action means IANA assigns codes only when a Standards Track RFC is published. Experimentation ranges are for vendors without IANA approval; implementations MAY ignore them. Vendor Private Use ranges let vendors extend OSPF with a vendor identifier embedded in the message.

Reserved ranges await future definition by Standards Track RFC or IESG-designated expert. The RFC uses RFC 2119 keywords: implementations MUST follow Standards Action assignments and SHOULD recognize vendor-private code points matching their vendor identifier.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to assign numbers. Some need a published standard. Others are for vendors to experiment. Some are reserved for the future.

sections.title: Core OSPF Registries
sections.content:
The RFC defines registries for OSPF messages. OSPFv2 Options and OSPFv3 Options are 8-bit and 24-bit fields indicating which features a router supports (multicast, external routes, NSSA). OSPF Packet Type (both versions) defines five core message types: Hello, Database Description, Link State Request, Link State Update, and Link State Ack.

OSPF Authentication Type specifies how routers prove legitimacy: values 0-2 assigned (none, password, MD5), ranges 3-247 for standards, 248-65519 reserved, 65520-65535 for experimentation. OSPFv2 Link State Type defines topology information kinds: Router-LSA, Network-LSA, Summary-LSAs, AS-external-LSA. OSPFv2 Router LSA Link Type distinguishes point-to-point, transit networks, stub networks, and virtual links.
sections.eli5: Different OSPF messages carry different kinds of information. These registries say which number means which kind.

sections.title: OSPFv3 and Extensibility
sections.content:
OSPFv3 (IPv6 OSPF) introduces LSA Function Codes: a numbering scheme combining three control bits with a 13-bit code. The U bit determines if an unrecognized LSA is flooded as understood (1) or treated as link-local only (0). S1 and S2 bits specify flooding scope: link-local, area, or AS-wide.

OSPFv3 Prefix Options indicate address prefix properties (unicast, link-local, multicast, propagate). OSPFv2 Opaque LSA Type and OSPFv2 Grace LSA Top Level TLV provide extension points with defined ranges for standards, experimentation, and vendor use.
sections.eli5: OSPFv3 lets routers tell each other how to handle unknown messages. These registries make sure extensions work together.

sections.title: Why This Matters for Security
sections.content:
RFC 4940 explicitly identifies poor IANA guidelines as a Denial of Service risk on OSPF and the standards process. Without clear policies, attackers or vendors could create code point collisions causing misinterpretation. Vendor Private Use ranges with embedded enterprise codes prevent accidental conflicts. Experimentation ranges protected from IANA assignment allow safe testing.

The RFC advises authors extending OSPF to examine extensions carefully and consider new registries or policies. By defining these registries in advance, RFC 4940 prevents exploitation and creates stable OSPF evolution.
sections.eli5: If code points were handed out randomly, routers would get confused. These registries prevent chaos and let vendors test features safely.

sections.title: How Registries Work in Practice
sections.content:
When implementing a new OSPF feature, determine which registry applies and check IANA for available code points. For published RFCs, request from Standards Action range. For experimentation, use Experimentation range without asking IANA. For vendor extensions, embed enterprise code and use Vendor Private Use code point.

At runtime, routers check code points and associated flags (U, S1, S2 bits in OSPFv3) to decide message handling. Unknown code points with U-bit set for understood are flooded; those set to ignore are discarded. This lets OSPF networks mix old and new implementations without breakage.
sections.eli5: When inventing OSPF features, pick a code point. For standards, IANA assigns. For experiments, use reserved numbers. For vendor-only features, mark them so others ignore them.
